newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Kohl visit highlights close but uneasy Czech ties.
newsitem.headline: Kohl visit highlights close but uneasy Czech ties.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl's visit to Prague on Tuesday to sign a landmark post-war reconciliation accord highlights the close but uneasy ties between the Czechs and their giant neighbour.

Kohl and Czech Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus are due to sign a joint declaration which both countries say is important for further European integration. But, with their often bloody past, the accord is highly controversial.
"The Czech-German conflict is part of the national consciousness, but the younger generation is already free of that," said Vladimir Nalevka, professor of history at Prague's Charles University.
The accord seeks to tie up the loose ends of World War Two and its aftermath and includes German support for Czech membership of the European Union and North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO).
Czech officials hope the declaration and a speech by Kohl, on his first visit to an independent Czech Republic, will give a fresh impetus to their plans to join both organisations.
"Through this, traditional animosities which have been repeated throughout our history can be overcome," said Nalevka.

Germany has been the chief political backer of the integration with the West of former East bloc states. However, the Czech Republic is the last of Germany's neighbours not to have signed a reconciliation agreement.
Germans and Czechs have rubbed shoulders for centuries. German was the common language of the Austro-Hungarian Empire, of which the Czech lands were part, and is still widely spoken.
Historically, Prague was a city of three peoples -- Czechs, Germans and Jews. Writer Franz Kafka, who lived in Prague, was a Jew who wrote in German.

But the war and the years that followed destroyed the tradition. The walls of Prague's Pinkas Synagogue is covered with the names of more than 75,000 names of victims of the Nazis. Today, the Jewish Quarter is mainly a museum.
After the war, Czech retribution came quickly. Some 2.5 million ethnic Germans were expelled and their property was confiscated.
Today, Germany is the Czech Republic's biggest Western trade partner and one of its biggest investors. German car giant Volkswagen owns former Czech car maker Skoda.
Both countries are soccer-mad -- Germany beat the Czechs in last year's European Championship final -- and both nations are proud of their beer.
In the accord, Bonn expresses sorrow for the 1938-45 Nazi occupation of the Czech lands and Prague expresses its regret for Czech brutality in the expulsions.
Both countries agree to set up a 160 million mark ($98.24 million) "Future Fund" to finance joint environmental, historical and other projects mainly to help victims of Nazi aggression.
However the accord has been criticised by families and supporters of the Sudeten Germans, mainly in Bavaria.
Czech communists and far-right Republicans plan demonstrations against the declaration in front of the Liechtenstein Palace, where it is to be signed, on Tuesday.
The party says the declaration underlines the German dominance of the Czech republic.
"We definitely will not support the declaration and we will welcome Chancellor Kohl in our own way," CTK news agency quoted Communist Party vice-chairman Zdenek Klanica as saying. ($1=1.6285 Mark)
